ai.definition: Digital twins for smart grids are virtual replicas of physical power networks that mirror their behavior and performance. These models enable real-time monitoring, simulation, and optimization to enhance grid reliability and efficiency.
ai.howItWorks: By creating detailed digital representations of the grid infrastructure, including substations, transmission lines, and distribution systems, digital twins can simulate various operational scenarios. This allows for predictive analysis, identifying potential issues before they affect the physical network, and optimizing energy flow based on real-time data.
ai.problemSolved: They address the challenges of maintaining a reliable and efficient power grid by providing tools to predict failures, optimize resource allocation, and enhance overall system resilience.
ai.manufacturing: Manufacturing involves developing and integrating sensors, IoT devices, and communication systems into the physical grid infrastructure. This data is then transmitted to cloud-based platforms where digital twin models are created and analyzed.
ai.buildProcess: The build process includes creating a detailed model of the grid, collecting real-time data from various sources, and using advanced analytics to simulate different operational conditions. Continuous updates are necessary as new data becomes available.
ai.costDrivers: Cost drivers include initial setup costs for sensors and IoT devices, ongoing maintenance and data processing expenses, and the need for skilled personnel to manage and analyze the digital twin models.
ai.lifecycleOutlook: The outlook is positive as more utilities recognize the benefits of predictive maintenance and real-time optimization. However, widespread adoption may be limited by initial investment costs and technical challenges.
ai.regulation: Regulatory frameworks vary by region but generally support the use of digital twins for improving grid reliability and efficiency. However, there are concerns about data privacy and security that need to be addressed.
ai.risks: Risks include cybersecurity threats to the digital twin system, potential inaccuracies in simulations leading to poor decision-making, and high initial costs deterring some utilities from adopting this technology.
ai.profitability: Profitability is variable but can be achieved through reduced maintenance costs, improved grid reliability, and enhanced customer satisfaction. The long-term benefits often outweigh the initial investment.
ai.futureDevelopment: Future developments may include more advanced AI algorithms for real-time decision-making, integration with other smart technologies like autonomous vehicles, and increased focus on sustainability and renewable energy sources.

glossary.def: A virtual replica of a physical system that mirrors its behavior in real-time, enabling predictive analysis and optimization.
An electrical power network that uses digital communication technology to detect and respond to changes in electricity supply and demand.
A strategy for maintaining equipment by performing repairs or replacements before a failure occurs, based on data analysis and modeling.

subsystems.name: Sensing and metering layer
subsystems.role: measures the real grid's state continuously.
parts: phasor measurement units (PMUs) on transmission lines
current and voltage transformers in substations

subsystems.name: Data transport and integration
subsystems.role: moves measurements to a central platform in real time.
parts: gateways speaking IEC 61850, DNP3 or MQTT

subsystems.name: Simulation and state estimation engine
subsystems.role: maintains a live, physics-based model of the grid.

subsystems.name: Analytics and optimisation
subsystems.role: turns the model into decisions: predict faults, reroute power, schedule maintenance.

subsystems.name: Visualisation and operator interface
subsystems.role: lets engineers see and interact with the twin.

subsystems.name: Control and actuation
subsystems.role: closes the loop by sending commands back to the physical grid.
parts: SCADA and energy management system (EMS) integration

buildSteps.title: Define scope and objectives
buildSteps.detail: Choose which part of the grid to twin — a single substation, a feeder, a region — and what the twin must do: predict failures, host more renewables, or cut losses.

buildSteps.title: Instrument the physical grid
buildSteps.detail: Install sensors, smart meters and PMUs on the chosen assets, or connect to existing SCADA and metering systems.

buildSteps.title: Build data pipelines
buildSteps.detail: Set up communications and a time-series database so measurements arrive continuously and are time-stamped and cleaned.

buildSteps.title: Create the base model
buildSteps.detail: Enter network topology, line and transformer impedances, generator data and load profiles into power-system simulation software.

buildSteps.title: Calibrate and validate
buildSteps.detail: Compare model outputs with real measurements and tune parameters until the twin matches the physical grid closely enough for the intended use.

buildSteps.title: Connect live data
buildSteps.detail: Stream real-time measurements into the model so state estimation runs every few seconds, keeping the twin synchronised.

buildSteps.title: Add analytics and interfaces
buildSteps.detail: Develop predictive maintenance, optimisation and visualisation tools on top of the live model, with clear alarms for operators.

buildSteps.title: Deploy and iterate
buildSteps.detail: Run the twin in parallel with the real grid, verify its advice against actual events, and expand its scope as confidence grows.

prerequisites.why: smart meters are widespread in some regions, but PMUs and asset sensors are not yet everywhere, so the twin sees only part of the grid.
fibre and 5G can carry the data, but many substations still rely on slow or intermittent links.

prerequisites.tech: Power-system simulation and state estimation software
prerequisites.why: decades of transmission-grid software provide the mathematical core the twin reuses.
IEC 61850 and the common information model (CIM) exist, but legacy equipment often needs translation layers.
the twin needs computing power to run thousands of simulations quickly, close to the data or in a data centre.
connecting a live model to control systems widens the attack surface, and protections are still maturing.

pathway.milestone: asset-level digital twins for transformers, cables and wind turbines
pathway.unlocks: condition-based maintenance that can delay or avoid costly replacements.

pathway.milestone: substation and feeder twins that simulate local outages and distributed energy resources
pathway.unlocks: faster fault location and better hosting of rooftop solar and electric-vehicle charging.

pathway.milestone: regional transmission and distribution twins running in real time
pathway.unlocks: predictive congestion management and coordinated voltage control across the whole network.

pathway.milestone: fully coupled twins that span generation, transmission, distribution and markets
pathway.unlocks: autonomous or highly automated grid operation with fewer blackouts and lower costs.
